newsitem.title: USA: Latin American debts mixed, Ecuador rebounds.
newsitem.headline: Latin American debts mixed, Ecuador rebounds.

text.p: Major Latin American Brady bonds were lightly mixed as market participants tried to sort out the implications of the wage ruling by Brazil's supreme court, traders said.

Brazil debt prices tumbled on Wednesday amid fears that Brazil's fiscal deficit would get out of control, if the court ruling that 11 federal civil servants were entitled to a 28.9 percent pay rise would be used as a precedent for claims by one million federal workers and pensioners.

Ernest Brown, Morgan Stanley's Latin America economist, estimated in a research report on Thursday that the full blown impact of a wage hike could widen Brazil's fiscal deficit by 0.7 percent of the gross domestic product and raise the inflation by one percentage point.
The executive branch will likely fight the ruling, but the outcome is far from being predictable, Fleury said.

Richard Segal, director of emerging market fixed income research, estimated the cost could go as high as $7 to $10 billion over two to three years, the impact on the economy would not be felt this year.
Traders said spreads for Brazil Bradies held largely steady, with the benchmark C bond widening about 5 basis points. Brazil C bonds were 1/4 weaker at 80-1/2.

Views on the future direction of C bond were divided, with some saying it was merely taking a pause after reaching a new high at 82.00 on Tuesday, and others predicting a substantial fall if the wage ruling should provide a catalyst, they said.
Argentina and Mexico were also affected by the uncertainties in Brazil, traders said.
Segal said Argentina's inflation is not closely correlated with Brazil, and the weakness was uncalled for.
Although a spate of buying pushed Brazil bonds higher earlier in London, activity slowed down when New York trading began, traders said.
"The market is suspiciously quiet," said Marcelo Fleury, vice president at the Brazil Desk of Garban Corp.
The wage ruling threw a monkey wrench into President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's economic plan built on low inflation, and low budget deficit, he said.
The wage increases could cost the government at least $6 billion, Fleury said.
Argentina pars were 1/4 lower at 67-3/4.
Mexico could have risen more on the strength of its gross domestic product report, if not for the cautious sentiment on Brazil, Segal said.
Mexico's economy grew a surprising 7.6 percent in the fourth quarter. With upward revision for previous quarters, the total GDP rose 5.1 percent in 1996, the government reported on Wednesday.

Under more benign market circumstmances, Mexico's debt papers would have also made more capital out of the announcement on Wednesday that it plans to pre-pay some $590 million loans to the International Monetary Fund, Segal said.
Mexico raised 50 billion yen in a seven-year Samurai bond, which, however, did not have impact on its dollar debt, traders said.
Ecuador Bradies got a lift, as it extended its bridge loan to six months from one month, giving the President Alarcon's government more breathing space, traders said.
Ecuador PDI rose 1-5/8 to 64-1/8 bid.
Bulgaria continued climbing, although traders could not point to particular news driving the market.
Bulgaria IAB firmed 1/4 to 59-1/8 bid.
